analysis.one_liner: Ends the loophole letting food companies self-certify questionable ingredients as safe without FDA review.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required FDA sign-off on "generally recognized as safe" food chemicals and mandated reassessment of substances including PFAS, phthalates, and titanium dioxide, was never taken up by the Senate committee it was referred to and died at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a food company can decide on its own that an ingredient is "generally recognized as safe" and put it in food without ever notifying the FDA. This bill would have ended that self-certification: companies would have to submit their safety evidence to the FDA, the determination would be posted publicly, and chemicals identified as causing cancer or reproductive harm could not qualify as safe. It also would have created a new FDA office required to reassess at least 10 substances every 3 years, starting with a named list of 10, including PFAS, phthalates, bisphenols, titanium dioxide, and potassium bromate [S2] [S3]. The bill was introduced by Senator Markey with three Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action on it before Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary food consumers, especially children, pregnant women, and other groups the bill defines as disproportionately vulnerable to chemical exposure. The bill requires safety factors for these populations, bans substances known to cause cancer or reproductive harm from the self-certified "safe" category, and orders reassessment of 10 specific chemicals of concern [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to submit their safety evidence to the FDA and get a written determination before marketing an ingredient as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS), instead of deciding on their own without notifying the agency [S2] [S3].

Prohibits substances identified by the National Toxicology Program as causing cancer or reproductive or developmental toxicity from being treated as GRAS, and requires safety factors protecting vulnerable populations such as infants, pregnant women, and the elderly [S3].

Creates an Office of Food Chemical Safety Reassessment at FDA that must reassess at least 10 substances or classes every 3 years, beginning with PFAS, ortho-phthalates, bisphenols, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, perchlorate, BHA, BHT, brominated vegetable oil, and propyl paraben [S3].

Makes FDA determinations and the supporting evidence publicly available, with a 90-day window for the public to object, and imposes conflict-of-interest standards on the experts providing data for GRAS reviews [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and the chemical ingredient suppliers they buy from. They would lose the ability to self-certify ingredients as safe without FDA review, would face a public posting of their safety submissions, and would bear the cost of reformulating products if chemicals on the reassessment list were found unsafe or restricted. Some of that cost could show up in food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food manufacturers and ingredient chemical suppliers

drawbacks.text: Food companies would bear new compliance costs: mandatory FDA submissions, waiting periods before marketing, and possible reformulation if reassessment found chemicals such as BHA, BHT, or titanium dioxide unsafe, with some of those costs likely passed to consumers [S3].

The bill orders a heavy, deadline-driven workload on FDA — a revised GRAS rule within a year and 10 full safety reassessments every 3 years — without an identified funding source, which an honest supporter would acknowledge could strain the agency's capacity [S3].
Defenders of the current GRAS system argue that self-certification keeps new ingredients and formulations reaching the market quickly; requiring case-by-case FDA review would slow that process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is closing a regulatory gap that lets companies put chemicals in food without FDA ever seeing the safety evidence, directly aimed at chemicals linked to cancer and harm to children's development. The costs are real but ordinary for a safety rule: compliance and reformulation expenses for the food industry and a demanding new workload for FDA. The main design risk is not the goal but the pace the bill imposes on the agency.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 26, 2022, with Blumenthal and Warren listed as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S3] [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the HELP Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers and chemical ingredient suppliers came out ahead: they continue to self-certify ingredients as "generally recognized as safe" without FDA notification or review, and the chemicals the bill would have reassessed remain in use as before. Consumers got no change in food chemical oversight.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction (one of three Democratic cosponsors listed).

against.name: Senate HELP Committee / Chair Patty Murray
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup was held and the bill was never reported to the full Senate.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill (3 of 48 Senate Democrats), but no vote ever occurred, so the record shows no opposition split to measure.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to self-certify ingredients as GRAS without FDA notification, would have their safety submissions posted publicly, and could face reformulation if listed chemicals were found unsafe. Their existing interest in unchecked self-certification runs against the bill's food-safety protections for consumers.

industries.industry: Food additive and chemical suppliers (including producers of PFAS, phthalates, bisphenols, and titanium dioxide for food uses)
industries.note: The bill named 10 substances for mandatory safety reassessment, and any found to induce cancer or reproductive toxicity would be deemed unsafe and barred. Suppliers of those specific chemicals had a direct financial stake in the bill dying.
